Port Forwarding — vazhi & Inspector Port Links

Features·seedling·accepted·JUL 25, 2026

A shared @kolu/port-forward library, the standalone vazhi TUI that proves it, and live openable port chips for every terminal in the Inspector — no new daemon.

Agents constantly start dev servers, and the URL scrolls away into the scrollback. This feature answers the one question kolu can’t answer today — where is the thing the agent just ran? — with exactly one concept: listening TCP ports, attributed to their terminal, one click from your browser.The inspiration, kero.sh, also shows a process list with CPU% and memory. We drop processes from the plan entirely (KISS): CPU% is the most expensive part to build for the least payoff, and a name+pid list is decoration. The process-subtree walk survives only inside the scanner, as the mechanism that attributes a port to a terminal. It ships as a shared library — @kolu/port-forward — consumed by two independent apps in the drishti mold: kolu’s Inspector, and vazhi (Tamil: way, passage), a standalone TUI in the spirit of opencode.

The plan is built for kolu’s real deployment shape: the server runs on a headless Linux box (pureintent) while the browser runs elsewhere (zest, a macbook on the tailnet). Everything below follows from one fact: “localhost” in a link means the viewer’s machine, so the only universally reachable place is the kolu server host — the name already in your address bar. Every port is made to answer there, and the client builds URLs from window.location.hostname, never a literal “localhost”.

How a click becomes a page — the three cases

where the server listens how it becomes reachable what the chip opens
kolu host, 127.0.0.1:5173 TCP relay: listen on 0.0.0.0:61000, pipe to loopback http://pureintent:61000
remote host, 127.0.0.1:5173 ssh -L *:61000:127.0.0.1:5173 on a connection of its own http://pureintent:61000
kolu host, 0.0.0.0:5173 already reachable — nothing to do http://pureintent:5173

In plain words: a dev server on pureintent’s loopback is invisible to your macbook (loopback never leaves a machine), so the library opens a door on pureintent’s network side and copies bytes across. A dev server on a remote host is one hop further: the same door on pureintent, with the ssh connection kolu already holds to that host carrying the last leg. And a server that bound 0.0.0.0 on pureintent needs no door at all — the scanner records the bind address, so kolu tells these cases apart automatically.Sub-case of case 2: the remote host is the viewer’s own machine (zest as a kolu remote host, viewed from zest). Traffic loops zest → pureintent → ssh → zest — roundabout but correct, and not worth a special case in v1.

One library, two apps — and no third daemon

kaval and padi remain the only daemons. The reusable capability is a library package, packages/port-forward/ (@kolu/port-forward): the forward map ((host, remotePort) → local listener, N hosts × N ports), one dedicated ssh -L process per remote forward, the loopback TCP relay, port picking, and teardown. For a remote target the local port is the remote port whenever that number is free here — pu-dev:4123 answers on 0.0.0.0:4123, a port you can predict and bookmark — and only when the number is taken does the kernel pick a free one instead; a forward is never refused merely because its number is busy, and there is no knob either way.Read the rule as remote-only: a local (loopback-relay) target never gets the preference and cannot, because both of its ends are on this machine — a listener on 0.0.0.0:<port> relaying to 127.0.0.1:<port> is pointed at ITSELF, and one connection to it opened ~29,000 file descriptors in 1.5s before the build caught it. The kernel always picks for a relay.

A forward lives exactly as long as the process that opened it. That is the one property the mechanism is chosen for, and it is why each forward gets its own ssh connection (ControlPath=none, so it can neither ride nor create a shared master) rather than a listener on a master shared with kolu. Sharing was the original design and it was wrong: OpenSSH gives a master’s forwards a lifetime of their own — a listener added with -O forward outlives its requester until the master’s ControlPersist idle timer reaps it, killing a mux client does not take its forward down, and there is no -O list, so a restarted process can neither see nor adopt what it left behind. An empty list beside live ports is the worst possible pair, and it is what the shared design actually produced.Both facts measured on a live sshd before the rewrite: forwards survived their creator by the full ControlPersist window, and a SIGKILLed mux client left its listener serving. Sharing a master and kernel-tied lifetime are mutually exclusive in OpenSSH; lifetime wins. The connection is held open by a remote command (cat) reading a pipe the library never writes to, so the kernel closing that pipe — on quit, on crash, on kill -9 — ends the session and with it the listener, with no timer in the loop.-N (no remote command) does NOT have this property: measured, an ssh -N -L child SURVIVES its parent’s SIGKILL and keeps serving the port. The hold-open command is what makes the lifetime kernel-tied, and a library test pins it — open a forward in a child process, SIGKILL it, require the port to refuse. The costs, stated: one ssh handshake per forward instead of a channel on a warm master, and a SIGKILL leaves the ssh children visible for as long as it takes their connections to notice — they die with those connections, they do not linger on a timer.

The per-forward connection also needs its own authentication, and that costs nothing new: kolu’s mirror already requires non-interactive ssh (BatchMode=yes and the rest of SSH_OPT_PAIRS), so any host kolu can mirror is a host a dedicated forward connection can reach with the same keys and the same ~/.ssh/config. host here is just an ssh destination — user@box, an alias, whatever kolu’s remote hosts already say — with no kolu-specific host model inside the library. And the ForwardManager API is the PRT2 contract: create (idempotent by target) · cancel · list · dispose · onLost is exactly what kolu’s Inspector will wire against, so the mechanism could be replaced under it — as it just was — without either app noticing. Mechanism in the library, policy in the consumers.Two shape questions PRT2 was to settle, and both settled as NO CHANGE — recorded because “we looked and the second consumer wanted the same thing” is a different fact from “nobody got round to it”. (1) list() stays pull-only. The prediction was that a second consumer would want a subscription; kolu instead does exactly what vazhi does — re-read the map after every act — and it does so because the surface CELL it feeds is itself a re-read on a change edge. Two independent consumers converging on pull is evidence the pull shape is right, not that the subscription is overdue. (2) create still rejects with the mechanism’s own message. The prediction was that the Inspector would branch on a kind (retry, pick another port, mark the host down); it branches on none of them, because the map ALREADY handles the only recoverable case — a taken local port falls back to a free one inside openPreferringPort, so it never reaches a consumer as an error. What is left is genuinely terminal (no ssh, host unreachable, tunnel never came up) and its one honest treatment is to show the user what happened. A tag with no reader would be speculative structure.

One thing DID change, and it went the other way — into the library rather than into a consumer: a target that comes back gets the local port it had before. That is what makes a link survive a dev-server restart, and it belongs to the MAP because it is bookkeeping the map already holds. Left to consumers, kolu and vazhi would each have kept the same table beside the same map and got its eviction rules subtly different.

Two consumers, no runtime link between them — the drishti pattern proper (shared libraries, independent apps):

  • kolu embeds the library in the server process it already runs. Forward state is a cell on kolu’s existing surface — no new socket, no IPC, no supervision. Kolu’s forwards live and die with kolu’s server, which is correct: reachability was tied to that process anyway.
  • vazhi is a standalone TUI (opencode-style — no CLI verbs, no serve mode) over the same library: a live table of its own forwards, add/cancel keybinds. Run it anywhere — including inside a kolu terminal, where kaval’s persistence keeps it alive across browser reloads for free. Kolu never consults it; it exists to prove the library stands alone and to manage forwards when kolu isn’t around. It gets its own flake.nix for later externalization into its own repo.Consequence of independence, stated: kolu and a running vazhi each own their own forwards and don’t see each other’s lists — they share nothing at all — not state, and (since each forward owns its own ssh connection) not connections either. Accepted for v1; a merged view would require the shared-daemon design this plan deliberately rejects.

Security posture, stated: a forward listener is unauthenticated raw TCP on the kolu server’s serving interface — anyone on the tailnet can connect, the same exposure as running the dev server on 0.0.0.0 yourself. That is the accepted v1 trust model (the tailnet is the trust boundary, as it already is for kolu’s own UI); per-forward auth would be a later, separate feature.

Port links in the Inspector

PORTS 3
🌐 5173 node ⤴ open ⇄ :61000
🌐 9229 node ⤴ open
🌐 61922 workerd ⤴ open
＋ Forward a port…
FORWARDED PORTS
⇄ pu-dev:5173 → :61000 · auto · ⨯   ⇄ zest:8080 → :61003 · manual · ⨯
vazhi — its own forwards, in its own terminal
pu-dev:3000 → 0.0.0.0:61010  up 12m
a add · x cancel · q quit

A Ports section joins the existing blocks in packages/client/src/right-panel/MetadataInspector.tsx (pure rendering — the data arrives on the terminal’s metadata like everything else). The flows:

  • Open. Click a chip → window.open on http://${location.hostname}:…, matching the Code tab’s external-open idiom (CodeTab.tsx:1114). Case-3 ports open directly; cases 1–2 call the embedded library’s create, get the listener port, open it, and the chip gains a ⇄ :61000 badge. Forwarding is lazy — first click only, never eager for every detected port.An agent session can hold six listening ports; auto-tunneling all of them VS-Code-style keeps idle listeners alive for ports nobody opens. Lazy costs one ssh handshake on first click — the price of a forward that dies with the process that opened it, and the reason to pay it once per opened port rather than once per detected one.
  • Manage. A Forwarded Ports group lists every active kolu forward — host:remotePort → :localPort, origin auto (chip click) or manual, cancel ⨯ per row. Kolu auto-cancels an auto forward when the scanner sees its remote port die; manual forwards persist until cancelled or their host disconnects. The same list appears in the host tab’s dropdown (beside state · terminals · padi·kaval), and the host tab itself carries a ⇄ n badge while forwards are live there: forwards are host-scoped, so the host popover is their natural home — each row a clickable http://… link with copy ⧉ and cancel ⨯ — while the Inspector group shows the same rows filtered to the active terminal’s host.
  • Manual forward. The ＋ Forward a port… row and a ⌘+K command accept host:port — for a port the scanner missed or one outside any terminal’s subtree.
  • The unit is the TILE, not the pane. A tile is one thing to the user and several PTYs to the daemon, so the scanner attributes a port to whichever pane’s subtree holds it — correct and unavoidable. But a dev server almost always runs in a split, so a section that read only the main pane showed nothing in the common case (observed on a live deployment during PRT1, not in review). Every ports surface therefore reads main + splits, the same unit the Attach section already documents, merging rather than grouping: which pane a listener sits in is a detail of how the user split their tile. PRT2’s Forwarded Ports group and auto-cancel inherit this — a forward belongs to the tile that opened it, not to a pane that may be closed while the server keeps running.
  • Discoverability. One tip in settings/tips.ts: “Click a port in the Inspector to open the server an agent just started.”

Detection: ports, attributed to the terminal

The scanner is its own package — @kolu/port-scan (packages/port-scan/, with the darwin C helper in its native/) — driven by a padi sensor, and not a kaval module. Two separate calls, and both matter.

Why a package: the OS is the volatility. How a kernel names the processes holding listening sockets has already changed three times on darwin in this repo alone, and linux answers by a different mechanism in a different byte order. That is the electricity bar — a real axis of change behind a stable receptacle — so the reader lives outside padi with the arrow pointing out, and its only input is a list of root pids. Test ③ (a second consumer proving it) is honestly still pending: the OSF standalone tool and PRT2’s vazhi are named but unbuilt, the same tier @kolu/serve-dir shipped at.

Why padi drives it: the repo’s own taxonomy draws the line. Facts that require the PTY itself live in kaval (foreground needs tcgetpgrp on the PTY fd, cwd is parsed from OSC sequences), while facts derived by OS inspection from a snapshot key live in padi (git status is derived from cwd; kaval knows nothing about git by design). The port scan needs zero PTY access — its only input is each shell’s root pid, which padi already reads off kaval’s list surface — so it sits beside the git sensor, keeps subprocess-spawning out of the memory-sensitive kaval, and changes no kaval wire contract (contract skew on remote hosts has its own bug note; not growing ptyHostSurface is a feature). One host-wide pass every 5 secondsCadence and the unref’d, non-overlapping poll shape copy packages/padi/src/memorySampler.ts and its derived.cell(source({ read, install: everyMsOr(…) })) wiring in servePadi.ts:247 — a padi idiom, which is one more reason the scanner lives there. builds the pid→ppid table once, partitions it into per-shell subtrees, and joins listening TCP sockets against each subtree:

  • linux — pid table from /proc/*/stat; LISTEN rows (with their bind address) from /proc/net/tcp + tcp6, joined to pids via /proc/<pid>/fd socket-inode readlinks (the same technique socketHolder.ts uses — RE-DERIVED, not shared: one leaf both plug into, with the fd-failure policy injected, is a standing extraction), walking only the union of terminal subtrees. Expect and tolerate per-pid EACCES/ENOENT outside the subtrees — but EACCES on a requested subtree surfaces as a scan error, never an empty port list. Do not spawn ss (measured ~7× slower, and it hides other-users’ pid attribution anyway).
  • darwin — a libproc helper kolu builds (packages/port-scan/native/portScanDarwin.c, compiled by the nix derivation beside it, its path baked onto padi as KOLU_PORT_SCAN_HELPER with no PATH fallback and no system fallback). ONE invocation prints BOTH tables in a versioned TSV — V\t1, then P\tpid\tppid\tname and L\tpid\tport\thex-bind-address (tab-separated) — and refuses a version it does not know, because a half-understood shape would parse to zero listeners and read as “nothing here is serving”. It emits raw address bytes, not a wildcard boolean, so isAnyAddress stays the single judge for both platforms; that hex is in NETWORK order where /proc’s is host-order-per-32-bit-word, which is why there are two decoders and exactly one judge. Non-root sees own-uid pids only — sufficient by construction, since a terminal’s subtree is padi’s own uid.This replaced ps + lsof, which had replaced netstat — and the netstat record has now been written up wrongly TWICE, in opposite directions, so it is stated as observations rather than as a verdict. Window A (the original): macOS 27.0 netstat -anv returns an empty internet table while reporting success — zero bytes, exit 0, clean stderr; -anv -f inet returns 117 bytes of header and no rows. Window B: on the same box the same /usr/sbin/netstat -anv -p tcp returns 29 LISTEN rows and -anv returns 241 KB — which was written up as “the original does not reproduce”, and the original was retracted. That retraction was wrong, and it made exactly the error it accused the original of: generalising one sampling window into an absolute. Window C (the adversarial fact-check) settled it — back to empty, deterministic over six back-to-back runs: -anv -p tcp 0 bytes / exit 0 / clean stderr, -anv 169 KB with zero tcp or udp rows (621 unix-domain rows — the internet tables are simply absent), and -anv -f inet 117 bytes, matching window A to the byte. A pty does not change it; lsof and the helper each saw the same 22 listeners at that moment; and the box had not rebooted between B and C (up 1 d 12 h, one boot). So macOS 27’s netstat intermittently loses its internet tables while reporting success — stable within a window, flipped between windows, cause unknown (three windows is not a mechanism, and command -v netstat resolved to /usr/sbin/netstat in every one). That is disqualifying by itself: “answers no ports, successfully” is the worst failure mode for a feature whose whole job is that question, and intermittent is worse than always. A second, independently verified reason stands too: netstat’s Local Address column is fixed-width and truncates (fe80::c051:5eff:.49508 — address cut, port glued on after a .), and the bind address is exactly what reachability is judged from.

The decided end state: one shared Rust helper, behind a proof gate

The C helper is deliberately not the destination. The destination is a small (~50-line) Rust binary wrapping sysinfo (pid / ppid / name) and listeners (pid plus the complete bind address — and on macOS it calls the same proc_listpids / proc_pidinfo / proc_pidfdinfo family directly rather than shelling out to lsof), owning the SAME versioned TSV above so the wire shape stays kolu’s and neither crate’s debug/Serde form leaks to a consumer. It is meant to become the kolu + drishti boundary in a subsequent PR, and that shared boundary — not speed — is what would justify it over two per-platform readers. It is not there yet; see the gate result below.

It ships when it passes a concrete gate, not before:

  1. Exact own-user listener parity — pid, port, address family, raw bind address — against ss on linux and this C helper plus lsof on macOS.
  2. Explicit fixtures for 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0, ::1, ::, and a dual-stack / IPv4-mapped listener. This is the specific known risk: listeners’ macOS address conversion does not visibly carry the insi_vflag & INI_IPV4 branch the C helper uses, and that branch is what makes a dual-stack :: socket classify as reachable rather than as needing a forward.
  3. A Node process reports as node, never a runtime thread name such as MainThread — executable basename must beat the short comm.
  4. Ten-run median ≤20 ms on both platforms at baseline, and max ≤40 ms with +100 listeners. This admits a low-tens Rust implementation and rejects a convenience wrapper with procs-like cost.
  5. Version line first; a malformed process name cannot change the field count; short stdout writes and top-level enumeration failures exit non-zero.
  6. A pinned dependency bump cannot merge without the parity tests on both platforms.

The gate RAN, and it FAILED on address parity — so the C helper ships

The ~50-line sysinfo+listeners wrapper was built and measured, not assessed on paper. It is not in this PR, because it did not clear the gate.

What failed: listeners drops the IPv4-mapping marker on darwin. Bind ::ffff:127.0.0.1 and ask every instrument about the same live socket — including the KERNEL, so this is not one tool’s word against another’s. Identical results from three independent binders (node, python3, and a raw C bind()) on zest, macOS 27.0:

instrument ::ffff:127.0.0.1 ::ffff:0.0.0.0
kernel getsockname — the arbiter 00000000000000000000ffff7f000001 → v4-mapped 32 zeros
kernel proc_pidfdinfo vflag=0x01 (INI_IPV4 set, INI_IPV6 clear) · v4 slot 7f000001 · v6 slot 0000…0000``7f000001 v4 slot 00000000
C helper (ships) 7f000001 ✓ 00000000 ✓
lsof 127.0.0.1 ✓ * ✓
sysinfo+listeners 0000000000000000000000007f000001 ✗ — i.e. ::127.0.0.1 32 zeros

Those ffff bytes are the mapping marker. Without them the reported address is ::127.0.0.1 — the deprecated IPv4-compatible address, which is a different address from the IPv4-mapped one that was bound. The C helper’s explicit insi_vflag & INI_IPV4 branch is what the crate is missing, exactly as the research predicted was the risk.

Severity, stated precisely: no wildcard verdict flips today. A mapped wildcard comes out as all-zeros, which isAnyAddress accepts via its all-zeros arm; a mapped loopback comes out non-zero and unmarked, which it rejects. So both classify correctly by accident. But two things are true and disqualifying: the address a consumer reads is wrong (PRT2 forwards to addresses, it does not merely classify them), and isAnyAddress’s v4-mapped arm — the arm that exists solely for this case — is then never exercised on darwin, so a future change to it would be untested on the one platform that needs it. Gate item 1 asks for exact raw-bind-address parity; this is not that.

What PASSED, so the follow-up need not re-derive it:

  • Linux parity and all five address fixtures: green, including the v4-mapped pair (linux reads /proc/net/tcp6, which carries the mapped form literally).
  • The crate’s integration tests run inside the nix sandbox on both platforms — verified, not assumed: loopback binds are permitted by linux’s private netns and by darwin’s sandbox-exec, and the darwin failure above was an assertion failure, not a bind error. So doCheck = true is viable wiring for the follow-up.
  • Latency was never the problem: the wrapper was in the same low-tens range as the C helper.

Three corrections to the research sketch, found by compiling it:

  1. listeners::get_all() returns UDP and non-listening sockets too (Protocol is TCP|UDP; SocketState carries the whole TCP state machine). The TCP && Listen filter is load-bearing — without it a UDP port, or an ESTABLISHED connection’s local port, is published as a listener.
  2. get_all() returns Box<dyn Error>, not Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>; the sketch’s main signature does not compile.
  3. sysinfo 0.39 requires Rust 1.95 while the pinned nixpkgs ships 1.93, so it pins to 0.37.

Round 2: the crate bug is FIXED in a fork, and the gate now fails on LATENCY only

The address bug was fixed and the gate re-run with the sound discriminator. Parity now passes everywhere; the blocker moved.

The fix. listeners is forked to juspay/listeners, branch fix/darwin-v4-mapped-addresses, rev 227440e922f8140f22b5a6966f28b387e3ce6e8a (pinned by rev, not branch, so a force-push cannot change what we build). It replaces the soi_family branch with an insi_vflag one. The flag ORDER is evidence-driven, and two measurements ruled out the simpler patches: a dual-stack :: sets both flags, so preferring v4 would report the wildcard as 0.0.0.0 and lose its IPv6 reach; and ::1’s v4 slot holds 00000001, which preferring v4 would surface as 0.0.0.1. Hence INI_IPV6 first, INI_IPV4 second, family last. A mapped bind now reports ::ffff:127.0.0.1, matching what the crate’s own Linux path already returns.

Two regression tests ride with it, negative-checked rather than assumed: the v4-mapped one FAILS on the unfixed code and passes after; the dual-stack one passes either way by design, because its job is to pin the flag order, which the first test cannot. Full crate suite on macOS: 15/16, and the one failure (test_consistency) fails identically with and without the fix — pre-existing, and diagnosed while we were there: lsof showed several ports on that host held by more than one process, so get_process_by_port(port) == a_specific_listener is not well-defined. Reported upstream as GyulyVGC/listeners#56 (bug report only — the decision to offer a PR is deliberately deferred).

Parity: PASS, on both platforms. Five fixtures × two binders (node, python3) × both platforms, oracles lsof + the C helper on darwin and ss on linux. Compared by the CORRECTED discriminator — canonical equivalence, not byte equality: v4-mapped → v4, and any all-zeros address → ANY (the same equivalence isAnyAddress itself applies, and a dual-stack wildcard is legitimately reportable in either width). 10/10 rows equal on each platform. The case that failed round 1 now reads …ffff7f000001 → v4:7f000001, equal to the C helper’s 7f000001.

Latency: FAIL, on both platforms. Gate is a 10-run median ≤20 ms:

median gate verdict
Rust wrapper, darwin (zest) 23.2 ms ≤20 ms ✗ over by ~3 ms
Rust wrapper, linux (550 procs) ~100 ms ≤20 ms ✗ over by 5×
C helper, darwin, same box + method 10.6 ms — the incumbent
padi’s own /proc reader, linux 14-18 ms — the incumbent

The +100-listener leg was not measured: the baseline already fails, so it could not change the verdict.

The cost is structural, not tuning. The wrapper enumerates processes twice — once via sysinfo, again inside listeners — where the C helper makes one libproc pass. That is exactly the risk the original research flagged. Worse on linux, and more fundamentally: listeners maps socket inodes by walking every process’s fds, whereas padi’s reader walks only the union of the terminal subtrees it was asked about. No amount of wrapper tuning changes that; it is the crate’s shape.

So the C helper still ships, and the decision that remains is a threshold one, not a correctness one. Darwin misses by ~3 ms for a readout whose cadence is duty-cycle bounded anyway (nudgeFloorMs would simply stretch its own floor). Linux is the real obstacle to the shared-boundary idea, and it is the platform that needs no helper at all. A plausible end state is therefore narrower than “one binary for both”: the shared boundary buys most of its value on darwin, and linux keeping its subtree-scoped /proc reader may be the right answer rather than a compromise. That is a call to make deliberately with these numbers in hand, not something to settle inside this PR.

Overturned: single-pass Rust matches C, so the shared binary is reopened

Surveying one more candidate — portview (MIT, v1.6.0) — produced a number that invalidates the conclusion drawn above, so it is recorded here rather than left in a report.

portview measured ~9.9 ms median on darwin and ~25.5 ms on linux, against our C helper’s 10.6 ms on the same box by the same method. It is Rust, and it is a single pass over its own libproc / /proc code.

So the sysinfo+listeners wrapper’s 23.2 ms darwin / ~100 ms linux was never Rust’s cost — it was the double enumeration, exactly as suspected: sysinfo walks the process list, then listeners walks it again (and on linux walks every process’s fds to map inodes). One pass in Rust is as fast as one pass in C.

That reopens the shared kolu ⇄ drishti binary on performance grounds. The blocker was never the language, and it was not really the crates either — it was composing two whole-host enumerations. A single-pass Rust binary written against the same libproc / /proc calls the C helper already uses should land in the same ~10 ms band, and it would carry the cross-platform boundary the C helper cannot.

That design is now written down in its own note — osfacts (proposed) — which also folds in memorySampler, socketHolder, the supervisor’s start-time reads and drishti, since they are all the same question asked five ways.

What that binary must add over portview, which is precisely what portview lacks:

  1. A process table, not just listener rows. portview emits one row per listening socket with a single ppid edge, so a shell → npm → node server cannot be walked back to its terminal: npm holds no listener and therefore never appears. That is the same disqualifier that ruled out portls, and it is the whole question this feature asks.
  2. --roots scoping, so cost tracks the ask rather than the host. portview’s single-port query is a host-wide scan followed by a filter — measured at 26.0 ms full vs 25.1 ms scoped, i.e. no saving at all.

Two smaller findings from the same survey, both already acted on:

  • portview does not shell out (own libproc//proc/IpHelper code), so it inherits neither the macOS netstat blindness nor the listeners v4-mapped bug — it reads insi_vflag. But it tests INI_IPV4 before INI_IPV6, so a dual-stack :: bind reports as 0.0.0.0 (predicted from its source, then measured on zest).
  • Our own C helper had that identical defect, and it is fixed in this PR — v6 is now tested first, with the dual-stack case bound and read back in the helper’s own install check. We do not get to hold an upstream project to a bar our own reader misses.

What the follow-up must clear, and the two things the fact-check corrected

The finding above survived an adversarial re-run whose explicit goal was to destroy it (fresh instruments, three binders — node, python3, a raw C bind() — and the kernel itself as arbiter). It also corrected two things, both of which the follow-up needs.

The gate’s discriminator was wrong, and it would have failed the C helper too. The original harness asserted BYTE-EQUALITY with …ffff7f000001. But the C helper emits 7f000001 for that same socket — a truthful, equivalent encoding of the same address in a different width, so it fails that assertion as well. The assertion conflated “same address” with “same encoding” and was not a sound discriminator. The gate must compare address EQUIVALENCE, canonicalising v4-mapped ↔ v4 (::ffff:a.b.c.d ≡ a.b.c.d), under which the C helper passes and the crate still fails. Byte-equality is the wrong test for a fact the OS is entitled to represent two ways.

The crate’s root cause is pinned, so the follow-up can file upstream from facts, not from a symptom. listeners 0.6.0 branches on soi_family — AF_INET6 means read the 16-byte insi_laddr.ina_6 slot — where it must branch on insi_vflag. For a v4-mapped bind macOS reports soi_family = AF_INET6 but insi_vflag = INI_IPV4 (v6 flag CLEAR), and it stores the address in the 4-byte i46a_addr4 slot while the v6 slot holds 12 zero pad bytes + the v4 address. Read as IPv6 that is ::127.0.0.1, the deprecated IPv4-compatible form — a different address from the IPv4-mapped one that was bound, which is what getsockname returns. Corroboration that this is the branch and not something else: the crate handles a plain 0.0.0.0 (AF_INET) socket correctly at 4 bytes, and its own Debug output names the wrong address outright ([::7f00:1]:19701).

So the fix is one insi_vflag & INI_IPV4 check in the crate’s macOS conversion — the same branch portScanDarwin.c already carries. Either land it upstream or apply it as a darwin post-process in the wrapper, then re-run the gate with the equivalence discriminator. If only latency ever fails, profile sysinfo’s second process pass — do not turn a one-shot sampler into a resident daemon merely to hide startup cost without revisiting the operational model.

The measurements the decision rests on — zest (macOS 27.0, ~826–866 processes), 10-run medians, spawn-to-exit; linux from a ~550-process workstation:

mechanism macOS median linux median
this C helper 8.45 ms · 9.41 ms with +100 listeners n/a — linux reads /proc directly (14–18 ms)
/bin/ps alone 49 ms —
/usr/sbin/lsof alone 94 ms —
procs --interval 1 29.6 ms — and it discards the bind address 89.8 ms
osqueryi union query not packaged for darwin 378 ms
portview (MIT, own libproc//proc code) 9.9 ms — but listener rows only, no process table 25.5 ms
sysinfo+listeners wrapper built and measured: low tens, but FAILS address parity (below) built; parity green

So the old darwin path spent ~143 ms of subprocess before parsing a byte, for facts libproc returns in one call — ps and lsof are themselves libproc clients. procs was rejected on function, not speed: it sorts and dedups u16 ports and throws the local IP away, so loopback-only and wildcard — the entire distinction this feature renders — collapse into the same row. osquery and rustnet were rejected on platform, size, and (for rustnet) its need for packet-capture privileges.

Re-measured on the shipped derivation: 10.6 ms/run on a busier zest (866 processes), with live lsof parity confirmed on all four bind shapes — including the dual-stack :: socket, where the helper’s INI_IPV4 branch yields the 4-byte 00000000 that isAnyAddress reads as reachable, matching lsof’s *:19304.

Attribution is the live ppid subtree — and nothing more. Backgrounded (&) processes, pipelines, and grandchildren all keep the shell as an ancestor, so the walk sees them; a true daemon (setsid/double-fork, reparented to init) leaves the subtree and is deliberately out of scope — no session-id heuristics, no host-wide orphan matching. If you daemonized it, it is no longer “this terminal’s server”.

Cadence: a 5-second baseline, nudged by output. The tick alone means up to ~5 s between a dev server’s “ready” banner and its chip — the one UX cost the spike numbers don’t excuse. So terminal-output bursts and OSC 633 command marks (the same signals the foreground sampler keys on) trigger an immediate off-schedule scan — single-flight, ≥1 s floor between passes — while the tick remains the baseline that catches quiet binds and port death (which auto-cancel in PRT2 rides on). Output is only ever a hint about when to look; the socket table stays the sole source of facts — a printed URL never creates a chip.VS Code’s output mode is the cautionary tale for crossing that line: its terminal-URL regex creates forwards with no liveness check, and its own settings text documents the consequence — bogus URLs yield stale forwards that survive until reload, and its process scanner exists only on Linux remotes (macOS/Windows get the regex, full stop). Most of its knob matrix — autoForwardPortsSource, the 20-forward hybrid fallback, per-port action overrides, focus-gated toasts — compensates for eager forwarding on uncertain evidence. Kolu’s lazy, scanner-derived design needs none of it.

Measured end-to-end through the shipped scanner (non-root): a complete linux scan is ~3 ms (~0.06% of a core at the 5 s cadence); the macOS pair is 17 ms on a quiet box and 93 ms on a busy one (~1.9% of a core). The 5-second cadence has room to spare on both.Parser subtleties, all fixture-worthy: /proc/net/tcp addresses are byte-reversed hex and IPv6 words are little-endian per 32-bit word, not across the address; v4-mapped IPv6 must be normalized (::ffff:0.0.0.0 is a wildcard, ::ffff:127.0.0.1 is not, and they differ in four bytes) and dual-stack rows deduplicated on the final structural PortInfo; a fork-inherited socket maps one inode to several pids, so attribution folds at subtree level before dedup; lsof brackets IPv6 hosts ([::1]:5173), which is what makes “port after the last colon” unambiguous, and spells the wildcard bind *. One more, found live: /proc/<pid>/stat’s comm is the THREAD name, and Node renames its main thread — a plain node dev server reports MainThread, so the displayed name comes from /proc/<pid>/cmdline’s argv[0] instead.

Each terminal’s sample — PortInfo { port, name, wildcard } in packages/terminal-vocab/src/schema.ts, beside ForegroundSchema:145 — is deduped by structural equality before it touches the snapshot, so an unchanged scan emits nothing: the churn guard that keeps a 5-second ticker from thrashing SolidJS. From there every layer exists: the sensor set folds it into TerminalSnapshot, the surface serves it (snapshot-then-deltas invariant, .claude/rules/streaming.md), and the reconcile-backed store in useTerminalMetadata.ts:180 delivers leaf-grained ticks to the section.

Architecture verdicts, conditioned on this build: the scanner is a leaf sensor module inside padi — a bounded one-shot scan with padi as its only consumer — and graduates only if it grows independent consumers or its own streaming volatility. @kolu/port-forward is the opposite case: ssh connection/forward lifecycle is a hard volatility with two genuinely independent apps on top (kolu and vazhi), which is exactly why it is a library package — the upstreamed “common stuff” of the drishti pattern — and why neither app is a daemon the other must talk to.

Build plan — the PRT track

What each phase changes for the user — the sentence you’d put in a release note:

  • PRT0 (shipped, #1975) — you can forward ports by hand, today, kolu or no kolu: run nix run …#vazhi in any terminal (a kolu terminal keeps it alive across reloads), type a host:4123, and get a live table with a clickable http://… link; q reaps every forward, guaranteed. Kolu’s own UI changes not at all.
  • PRT1 (shipped, #1982) — the Inspector answers “what is this terminal serving?”: a live Ports section lists every listening port of the session within seconds of it appearing. No forwarding yet — but a port bound to 0.0.0.0 on the kolu server host needs none (it already answers on the name in your address bar), so those chips open in one click; loopback-bound and remote-host ports are listed but wait for PRT2.
  • PRT2 (shipped, #1991) — every port is one click from a page, wherever it lives: loopback and remote-host ports open via automatic forwards, a Forwarded Ports group shows and cancels them (plus a manual ⌘K “Forward a port…”), and forwards clean themselves up when the server dies. This is the headline: the agent started something → you’re looking at it.
  • PRT3 (deferred) — the page opens inside kolu instead of a browser tab.
id ships needs proof
PRT0 ✅ @kolu/port-forward library + vazhi TUI — #1975 — standalone forward on a real remote box, no kolu running
PRT1 ✅ padi port sensor · Ports section · direct open — #1982 — e2e: spawned listener’s chip appears + opens
PRT2 ✅ kolu embeds the library — #1991: lazy forward · Forwarded Ports UI · manual · auto-cancel PRT0 + PRT1 real remote box: chip → tunneled HTTP 200; kill the server → ports refuse
PRT3 embedded in-kolu preview pane PRT2 deferred — not planned yet

PRT0 shipped in #1975 and PRT1 in #1982; PRT2 shipped in #1991; PRT3 is the only phase left, and it is deferred by design.

PRT0 — the library, proven by vazhi (shipped: #1975)

packages/port-forward/ plus the vazhi TUI with its own flake.nix (nix run .#vazhi). Done when, with no kolu running: in a terminal, vazhi adds a forward to a real remote box (pu harness) and shows the row live; curl http://<vazhi-host>:<port> from a different machine returns the remote server’s body (proving the non-loopback bind); cancelling the row severs it; quitting vazhi tears its forwards down. Two structural criteria on top: vazhi imports only @kolu/port-forward (no kolu internals) — the proof that makes PRT2’s embed mechanical — and kill -9 on vazhi leaves no port answering, checked immediately rather than after any timer, which is the property the per-forward connection exists to give.

PRT1 — detection + Ports section (shipped: #1982)

Scanner, ports schema field, sensor fold, the Inspector section, direct-open chips, the tip. The shipped mechanisms — the linux /proc reader and the darwin C helper — have a designed successor: one shared Rust binary serving kolu and drishti, planned in osfacts; until it passes that note’s gates, what ships here is the measured best on each platform. Done when an e2e scenario runs node -e 'require("http").createServer((_,r)=>r.end("ok")).listen(8123,"0.0.0.0")' in a real kolu terminal and asserts the 8123 chip appears within two scan ticks and clicking it opens the page at location.hostname:8123 — pinning the real path (padi scan → snapshot → surface → reconcile store), which no client-side mock can satisfy. Parser unit tests run on fixture /proc trees and fixture lsof field output; the darwin gate (aarch64-darwin) must be green, not skipped. Loopback-bound chips render with a “needs a forward” affordance; PRT2 made it live.

Fixtures are not enough, and this phase proved it twice. A fixture pins the parser; it cannot pin the assumption that the parser is handed the shape it expects — and both darwin bugs lived exactly there, green fixtures over a scan that threw or saw nothing. So the scanner also carries a live suite that spawns real listeners and asks the real scanner about them on whatever platform it runs (describeDaemon-gated, so it rides the ci::daemon node that is required on both platforms).

Scanner discipline, pinned from the Zed/VS Code comparisons: the pass holds no OS state between ticks — parse, join, emit the structural PortInfo snapshot, drop everything else (no retained fds, no process objects, no thread enumeration); it repartitions from the current terminal root pids every tick, so a terminal opening, closing, or being re-keyed never leaves a stale subtree; and it is single-flight (the output-nudge and the baseline tick share one non-overlapping runner).

PRT2 — kolu embeds the library (shipped: #1991)

⇄ Forward a port… host:port → opens a tunnel

What ships, at a glance — detail lives in the footnotes:

  • Every chip opens. Click → the embedded library opens a door → new tab at http://${location.hostname}:<port>. Lazy, first click only.Case-3 (wildcard on the kolu host) keeps opening directly with no door. Cases 1–2 call create and the chip gains a ⇄ :<localPort> badge. Lazy because an agent session can hold six listening ports; eager VS-Code-style tunneling keeps doors open for ports nobody visits, and their knob matrix exists to walk that back.
  • Two door mechanisms, both shipped in PRT0 and vazhi-proven: an in-process TCP relay for the kolu host’s own loopback ports, one dedicated ssh -L child per remote forward.The ssh child runs with ControlPath=none plus a hold-open remote command — it can neither ride nor create a shared master, so the forward’s lifetime IS the child’s lifetime. The shared-master design was measured and rejected in PRT0: -O forward listeners outlive their requester by the full ControlPersist window, and OpenSSH has no -O list to re-adopt them.
  • Same port when free: box:5173 answers at :5173, predictable and bookmarkable; the kernel picks only on collision — and a restarted listener gets its old local port back.The restart rule is one of two details adopted from VS Code’s Ports view; the other is copy-address on every row. Both exist so links survive a dev-server restart.
  • Forwarded Ports, three surfaces: a group in the Inspector (active terminal’s host), the same list in the host tab’s dropdown, and a ⇄ n badge on the host tab itself whenever that host has live forwards — glanceable from anywhere.Forwards are host-scoped facts, so the host popover is their natural home; the Inspector group is the same rows filtered to the active terminal’s host. Rows: host:remotePort → :localPort · auto|manual · ⧉ copy · ⨯ cancel, each a clickable link.
  • ⌘K: “Forward a port…” — accepts host:port, for anything the scanner missed or outside any terminal’s subtree.
  • Doors close themselves. Scanner sees the port die → auto forwards cancel; manual ones persist until cancelled or the host disconnects; kolu killed → the kernel closes everything, instantly.The kolu-level twin of vazhi’s SIGKILL criterion, and it matters MORE here: the server restarts on every deploy. The old shared-master design would have orphaned every forward on each release while the restarted UI showed an empty list.

The deferred shape question, settled: wildcard became scope

PRT1’s review left one question open for exactly this phase — whether PortInfo should carry wildcard: boolean or a three-way scope: "any" | "loopback" | "interface" — on the grounds that PRT2 is where the second consumer appears and the tag could then be designed against two real readers instead of one. It appeared, and the boolean was wrong for a reason no amount of structural argument had reached: it is not a distinction the MECHANISMS can act on.

Both of PRT0’s doors connect to 127.0.0.1 on the far side — the relay dials this machine’s loopback, the ssh -L child dials the remote’s. So the boolean’s false arm covered two cases with opposite correct handling: a loopback bind (exactly what a door reaches) and a bind to one specific interface such as 192.168.1.5 (which answers at that address, and which no door can reach at all). Under wildcard: boolean the second case rendered as “needs a forward”, the click would open a listener successfully, and every connection through it would be refused. A boolean cannot spell the difference, so PRT2 ships the three-way and portReach grows a fourth, honest arm — no-mechanism — that offers nothing because there is nothing to offer.The reshape is one classifier, not a schema patch: isAnyAddress became addressScope, still the SINGLE judge both platforms reach through their own decoder, so the two cannot come to disagree about ::ffff:0.0.0.0 — the property PRT1 paid for twice. The fold widens rather than ORs (any > interface > loopback), which keeps it order-independent, which is what keeps a 5-second scanner from republishing a “change” forever. Cost, stated: padi’s surface goes 4.2 → 4.3 and a straddling padi is drained by the existing convergence machinery before either parser meets the other’s frame — the same rule 4.1 and 4.2 already rest on, so the reshape needs no compatibility arm and deliberately has none. Verified against the real OS, not just fixtures: the live suite binds a real routable interface address and asserts it classifies as interface.

The structural lens’s original case stands too, and is worth recording as separate: scope is still an OBSERVATION, not a verdict. Whether a port answers for a given viewer needs the HOST as well, which no field of PortInfo ever carried — so the judgment stays portReach(scope, onKoluHost) in kolu’s own vocabulary, where both ends of the wire read the one copy.

…and then production froze, and scope turned out to be half the fact

The first deploy of PRT2 froze the entire kolu server on the first forward click — UI dead, HTTP dead, SIGTERM ignored until systemd sent SIGKILL — and the forward it did open served nothing. Three defects, and the two that matter are the same mistake in different clothes.

The freeze was a cycle between two reasonable halves. The forward cell is a poll on a fused cadence (everyMsOr(interval, onChange)): the interval runs the auto-cancel pass, and the change edge makes an act publish at once instead of waiting out a tick. Separately, the auto-cancel pass ended by announcing its result. Each half is right on its own; together, the pass announced on the very edge that triggers the pass — read → reap → announce → tick → read — and the event loop never yielded again. It was invisible until the first click because with zero auto forwards the pass returned before announcing. The fix is not a guard on the announcement but the removal of the shape: the reconciliation reports by returning, the poll publishes what it returns, and “reap and announce” is no longer spellable.The general lesson is worth more than the fix: neither module was wrong in isolation, so no unit test of either could have caught it. What catches it is a test of the JOIN — the regression test reproduces the fusion in miniature and asserts the read count stays BOUNDED, which is a property of the wiring rather than of any module in it.

And scope was half a fact. 127.0.0.1 and ::1 are both loopback and are not the same address; the classifier folded them together, and both mechanisms then dialled v4. A dev server on [::1]:5173 — what vite and several Node versions bind by default — got a tunnel that came up perfectly and served nothing, because there was no listener at the address the door opened onto. So PortInfo now carries family beside scope, and it is a separate field rather than a fourth scope value because the two answer different questions: scope decides whether a door is needed, family decides what it dials, and only the first is a reachability judgment with an ordering.

The two are one lesson, stated once because it has now cost two defects in one PR: a fact the OS handed us was collapsed below what the consumer needed, and the collapse was invisible until something dialled the answer. wildcard lost the interface case; scope lost the family. Both looked like tidy reductions and both were reductions past the point of use.Which is why the dial family is now read SERVER-side off kolu’s own scan rather than accepted from the client: a client’s copy of the port facts can be a scan or two stale, and a stale family opens a door onto an address with nothing behind it — the same failure by a different route. The one place kolu cannot observe it (a manual forward to a port no terminal serves) assumes v4 at a single named constant, with the failure loud at the point of use rather than silent.

A second question of the same shape was RAISED AND SETTLED IN PRT1, not deferred: whether a terminal that has never been successfully scanned is distinguishable on the wire from one that serves nothing. It was first argued as unreachable and the peer review refuted that with three surviving routes — a first-pass lsof timeout on darwin, a transient /proc/net/tcp read failure on linux, and (widened by PRT1’s own fix) any unexpected /proc errno — none of which needs the terminal’s own shell to be unreadable. So ports is a discriminated known / unknown two-way, the same honest shape ProcessRss already uses, and holding a last-good sample now covers only what it can actually cover.PRT1 also left a second, smaller judgment on the table: kaval’s one host-global activity edge now has three independent resubscribeStream consumers (the finish fold, the live dots, the port-scan nudge). They are not three copies of one shape — the live-dots one is per-SUBSCRIBER by design, the other two are daemon-lifetime — so the shared fan-out waits for a consumer that actually matches, rather than forcing the per-subscriber case into a receptacle it does not want.

The kolu server embeds @kolu/port-forward; forward state becomes a cell on kolu’s existing surface; chip click → lazy create; tunnel badges; Forwarded Ports group; manual forward + ⌘K command; auto-cancel policy. Two UX details adopted from VS Code’s Ports view: when an auto-forwarded listener dies and later returns, re-forwarding prefers the local port it had before (links and bookmarks keep working across a dev-server restart), and every forwarded-port row carries a copy-address affordance beside open and cancel. Done when, verified with the remote-host-testing harness against a real remote box and a viewer on a different machine than the kolu server: clicking a remote terminal’s chip creates the forward through the embedded library (a running vazhi is neither required nor consulted), the opened http://<kolu-host>:<localPort> returns the remote server’s body, cancelling the row severs it, and stopping the remote server auto-cancels the auto forward within two scan ticks. Plus the kolu-level twin of PRT0’s SIGKILL criterion, which matters MORE here than in vazhi because the server restarts on every deploy: kill the kolu server and every forward it created must refuse connections at once — the old shared-master design would have orphaned them on each release while the restarted Inspector showed an empty list. Evidence video of the click-to-page flow.

When the viewer IS the host. A machine in kolu’s fleet can be the machine you are reading kolu from — the plan’s own footnote called this “roundabout but correct, and not worth a special case in v1”, and in practice it was baffling: every chip on zest’s terminals, viewed from zest, offered to open a door on pureintent so that zest’s browser could reach a port on zest. So kolu now recognises it, from the one fact that can settle it: the peer address of the viewer’s own connection, which only the server can see, compared against the addresses the host resolves to.

Two things make an inexact comparison acceptable here, and neither is incidental. First, the failure direction is safe: a match opens the port directly on the viewer’s own loopback, and every way of failing to recognise the viewer — a NAT, a proxy, an ssh alias DNS cannot resolve — leaves the forward exactly as it was, which works. Second, a direct port is never rewritten to localhost: it already answers on a name that means the same thing from every machine, and localhost is the one hostname that does not — trading the first for the second would undo the rule this whole feature is built on.

It rides a ROOT rpc rather than a surface member, and that is structural rather than convenient: the answer differs per viewer, and a surface cell is broadcast, so it has no shape that can carry a different answer to each connected browser.The reliable version of this needs a fact kolu does not have — the host’s own interface addresses, which padi could report but does not — so what ships resolves the ssh destination instead. That is genuinely weaker for alias-named hosts, where it simply never fires. Recorded as a limit rather than hidden, because the alternative was to add a padi surface field inside an incident fix.

The first cut of it never fired once, and the reason is worth keeping. It compared the connection’s TCP peer — and kolu’s real deployment is reached through tailscale serve, which terminates TLS and dials the backend from the host’s OWN tailnet address. So the only established connection to kolu had peer 100.122.32.106: pureintent itself. The viewer’s address never appeared as a TCP peer at all; it was in an X-Forwarded-For header nothing read. The comparison had been right the whole time and the observation feeding it belonged to the proxy.

So the address is now taken from the forwarded header when, and only when, the direct peer is a trusted local hop — loopback, or one of this host’s own addresses, which is exactly what a local reverse proxy looks like. Three properties make that safe to state as a rule rather than a setting: a header arriving on an untrusted connection is ignored entirely (anyone who can reach kolu directly can invent one, and honouring it would let a stranger be handed a localhost link for any host’s ports); the last entry wins rather than the first, because each proxy appends the address it received from while the leftmost entry is whatever the client typed; and there is no trusted-proxy list to configure, because the trust condition is a fact about the connection rather than a knob.A deployment shape that hides the viewer more thoroughly — a proxy on a different machine, or one that strips the header — lands on the same no-match side as before, which keeps the forward that works. The mechanism is allowed to not fire; it is not allowed to be wrong.

What the automated suite actually covers, and what it deliberately does not. The e2e scenarios drive the relay case end to end — a real loopback listener in a real PTY, a real click, and the listener’s own body arriving in the opened tab through a port it never bound — plus the cancel twin, which proves the door is shut by dialling the recorded URL from node rather than by watching a row disappear. The ssh -L case is not simulated: it needs a second machine, and a loopback ssh hop standing in for one would exercise a different code path from the one it claimed to cover, so it stays with the remote-host-testing harness above. Stated rather than left implicit, because “the port forwarding suite is green” would otherwise read as covering both mechanisms.

PRT3 — embedded preview (deferred)

Open the forwarded page inside kolu — a browser pane in the Code tab, in the spirit of the Codex desktop app — instead of a new tab. Explicitly out of scope until PRT2 shippedA cross-origin iframe surface for arbitrary dev servers is a genuinely bigger build, and any server sending X-Frame-Options: DENY / frame-ancestors refuses framing — the new-tab path must remain the fallback regardless.; no design here yet — when it matures this section is rewritten, not layered.
